title: When someone dies: what to do and who to call
description: What happens when a Muslim dies in Canada, who to call first, the paperwork with Ontario as the example, and how a convert can protect their own wishes.
intro: Muslims bury their dead quickly, so the first hours matter. Born Muslims often learn the steps from family. You may be the only Muslim in your household, so this guide sets out what happens, who to call and what to say. It ends with a short checklist for protecting your own wishes. This is general information, not legal advice, and the details of washing, shrouding and the funeral prayer should be checked with your imam.
summary: Save your masjid's funeral contact in your phone now, before you need it.
If a death is expected, the doctor or nurse confirms it. If it is sudden, call 911.
Tell the hospital or the coroner straight away that the family wants a Muslim burial and that timing matters.
A masjid funeral service usually handles the washing, the shroud, the paperwork and the burial.
Your non-Muslim family may make the decisions after your death, so put your wishes in writing and name an executor who will follow them.

sections.heading: Save one number now
sections.body:
Ask your masjid whether it has a funeral committee or works with a Muslim funeral service, and save that number in your phone. Many masjids run one. The Scarborough Muslim Association in Toronto, for example, lists body release, washing and shrouding, cold storage, the death registration, the burial permit and burial at a Muslim cemetery. That is one example of the kind of service to look for, not a recommendation.

If your masjid does not offer this, ask which service it uses. A regular funeral home may not know what a Muslim burial needs, so the masjid's contact is the one to call first.

sections.heading: What to do in the first hours
items: If the death was expected, at home or in hospital, a doctor or nurse confirms it.
If the death was sudden or unexpected, call 911.
Tell the hospital staff or the coroner right away that the family wants a Muslim burial and why timing matters.
Call the masjid funeral contact. They explain the next steps, the paperwork and the cemetery.
If you are not the next of kin, stay close and offer to make the calls. The family decides.

sections.heading: The Islamic steps in plain words
sections.body:
First the body is washed (ghusl of the deceased), usually by trained volunteers from the masjid. Then it is wrapped in plain cloth (the shroud, kafan). The community prays the funeral prayer (salat al-janazah), and the burial follows as soon as it can be arranged. Muslims do not cremate.

The funeral prayer is short. Everyone stands in rows behind the imam and there is no bowing or prostration. There are four takbirs (saying Allahu Akbar). In the method IslamQA teaches, you recite Al-Fatihah after the first, send blessings on the Prophet after the second, make dua for the person who died after the third, then say the fourth takbir and end with the salam. The schools differ on the words after the first takbir and on the number of salams, so follow the imam and ask him about your school.

The details of washing and shrouding also differ between the schools. The masjid team knows them, and you do not need to learn them before you help.

sections.heading: The paperwork, with Ontario as the example
sections.body:
Each province has its own offices and forms. In Ontario, the province's guide sets out these steps. A doctor or nurse practitioner completes the Medical Certificate of Death. A Statement of Death is filled in with the person's details. The death is registered with the municipality, which issues a burial permit. The province also says families can make the arrangements without a funeral service provider, although most people use a masjid service or a funeral home.

In other provinces, ask the masjid service or the hospital which forms apply. The Government of Canada has a checklist for what comes after, such as telling federal programmes about the death, benefits, and estates and wills.

sections.heading: Sudden deaths and the coroner
sections.body:
A coroner looks into deaths that are sudden or unexpected. Ontario's coroner service asks families to say straight away if they have religious or cultural needs about timing, and the coroner considers those concerns. The decision on whether to do an autopsy belongs to the coroner, and in Ontario it is legal and binding.

An autopsy can delay the burial, but the washing, the funeral prayer and the burial still happen once the body is released. Speak up early and calmly, and let the masjid service talk to the coroner's office if that helps.

sections.heading: Cemeteries and costs
sections.body: Some areas have Muslim cemeteries and others have a Muslim section in a municipal cemetery. Ask your masjid which one it uses and what a plot and the service cost, because prices differ a lot between cities. If money is a worry, say so. Many masjids know where to find help for a family that cannot pay.

sections.heading: Women and the funeral
sections.body: Women can attend the funeral prayer. Whether women follow the procession and attend the burial is discussed differently in the schools, and masjids have their own practice. Yaqeen Institute's series For Those Left Behind has an episode on women praying the funeral prayer and visiting graves. Ask your masjid what it does, and ask your imam about your school.

sections.heading: Protect your wishes: a checklist for converts
sections.body: After you die, your legal next of kin may not be Muslim. In most provinces they, or the executor of your will, make the decisions about your body and your funeral. Without written wishes and an executor who agrees to follow them, a Muslim burial may not happen. This is worth doing quietly, now, even if you are young and well.
items: Write one short paragraph saying you are Muslim and want a Muslim burial. A sample is in the scripts below.
Make a will that names an executor (called an estate trustee in Ontario) who has agreed to arrange a Muslim burial. Ask them first.
Tell one Muslim friend and one family member where your will and your written wishes are.
Put your masjid's funeral contact in your phone and in the note.
Tell your family kindly, when it feels safe, so it is not a surprise.

sections.heading: Who decides in your province
sections.body:
This depends on provincial law, and the rules differ.

In British Columbia, the Cremation, Interment and Funeral Services Act gives the right to decide first to the executor named in the will, then to the spouse, an adult child and other relatives in order (section 5). A written preference in a will or a preneed funeral contract is binding unless it is unreasonable, impracticable or a hardship (section 6).

In Ontario, the province's guide does not say who controls the funeral. Lawyers usually describe the estate trustee as the person with that right and written burial wishes as guidance that is not binding. We have not confirmed this from a primary legal source, so ask an Ontario lawyer. If it is right, naming an estate trustee who will honour a Muslim burial matters more than the written note.

In other provinces, ask a lawyer how it works where you live. Our wills and inheritance topic has more on making a will.

sections.heading: If your wishes are not followed
sections.body:
Some converts worry that their family will cremate them. An answer from IslamWeb's fatwa centre to a convert with this fear says she should put her wishes in writing and give them to Muslims who will carry them out, and that she carries no sin if her family cremates her against her will. Do what you can, then leave the rest to Allah.

If your conversion is still private, keep the note somewhere safe or with a Muslim friend. Our red flags and staying safe guide has a section on keeping your conversion private.

scripts.title: Calling the masjid
scripts.body: Assalamu alaikum. My name is ___. Someone in my family has died at ___ (hospital or address). We want a Muslim burial. Can you tell me what to do next and who will handle the washing and the paperwork?

scripts.title: Telling the hospital or the coroner
scripts.body: The family wants a Muslim burial. In our faith the burial happens as soon as possible, so please tell us early about any steps that could cause a delay. This is the phone number of our masjid's funeral service.

scripts.title: Your written wishes
scripts.body: I am Muslim. When I die, I wish to be washed, shrouded and buried according to Islamic practice, and not cremated. Please contact ___ (masjid and phone number), who will help with the arrangements. Signed ___, dated ___.

scripts.title: Telling your family
scripts.body: This is not because anything is wrong. I just want you to know that if something happens to me, I would like a Muslim burial. The masjid can take care of the details. I have written it down so nobody has to guess.

scenarios.title: Your Muslim spouse dies suddenly at home.
scenarios.response: Call 911 first. When the police or paramedics arrive, say you want a Muslim burial. Then call the masjid funeral contact. The coroner may be involved, so tell the coroner's office about timing early.

scenarios.title: The coroner orders an autopsy.
scenarios.response: The coroner's decision stands, and a Muslim burial still goes ahead afterwards. Ask how long it will take, and let the masjid service keep in touch with the coroner's office.

scenarios.title: You do not have a masjid yet.
scenarios.response: Use our masjid finder to find the nearest one and call the office. Even if you have never visited, they will help or tell you who to call.

scenarios.title: Your parents ask what you would want if you died.
scenarios.response: Take the question as care. Tell them simply that you would like a Muslim burial, and say where your written wishes are.

title: Having a baby as a new Muslim
description: What Muslims do when a baby is born, what is sunnah and what is family custom, names, aqiqah, circumcision under Canadian medical guidance, and your mood after the birth.
intro: A new baby brings a lot of advice, some of it religious and some of it family custom. This guide sets out the practices Muslims follow after a birth, how strongly each one is recommended, and where Canadian health guidance comes in. None of it has to be perfect. Ask your imam about your school, and your doctor or midwife about your health and your baby's.
summary: The recommended acts after a birth are sunnah, not conditions of your child being Muslim.
The aqiqah is a confirmed sunnah for those who can afford it. It is not a debt if you cannot.
A good name matters. It does not have to be Arabic.
If you want your son circumcised, ask your doctor early. Provincial plans do not pay when it is done for religious reasons.
Low mood or anxiety after a birth is common and treatable. It is not a faith problem.

sections.heading: Sunnah, custom and what can wait
sections.body: Relatives and in-laws may present their customs as religious duties. Some are sunnah, some are culture, and some are both. It is fine to ask kindly, "Is this from the religion or from the family?" and to check with a teacher. Customs such as a forty-day rest for the mother vary a lot between families and countries.

sections.heading: The first days: acts Muslims follow
sections.body: SeekersGuidance, answering from the Shafi'i school, lists these recommended acts. They are good to do, and missing one does not make anything invalid.
items: The call to prayer (adhan) in the baby's right ear, and the iqamah in the left.
Putting a little softened date in the baby's mouth (tahnik). Check with your midwife or doctor before giving a newborn any food.
Choosing a good name.
On the seventh day, shaving the baby's head and giving charity.
The aqiqah, an animal sacrifice to thank Allah for the child.

sections.heading: How strong is the adhan hadith?
sections.body: The report that the Prophet gave the call to prayer in his grandson's ear is in Sunan Abi Dawud 5105, graded Hasan by Al-Albani. At-Tirmidhi also narrated it (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1514) and called it hasan sahih, while the Darussalam grading on Sunnah.com is Da'if. So the strength of the report is debated, and the schools do not all treat the practice the same way. The same SeekersGuidance answer says whispering the baby's name in the ear is not an established sunnah. Ask your imam what your school holds.

sections.heading: The aqiqah
sections.body:
IslamWeb's fatwa centre calls the aqiqah a confirmed sunnah for those who can afford it: two sheep for a boy and one for a girl, on the seventh day, or otherwise the fourteenth or twenty-first, or any time before the child reaches puberty. The schools differ on how strongly it is recommended. It is not an obligation, and nobody should borrow money to do it.

Some charities and halal butchers can arrange an aqiqah for you. Ask your masjid who it trusts.

sections.heading: Choosing a name
sections.body: Choose a name with a good meaning. It does not have to be Arabic, in the same way that converts usually keep their own names unless the meaning is a problem. If you like a name but are unsure what it means, ask someone who knows the language before you decide.

sections.heading: Circumcision for baby boys
sections.body:
The schools of Islamic law differ on male circumcision: some treat it as strongly recommended and others as required. Our questions page covers what this means for adults.

For babies, the Canadian Paediatric Society's parent handout (last updated in February 2021) says the CPS does not recommend circumcising every newborn boy as routine care, and that many parents choose it for religious reasons. It should be done by a trained, experienced practitioner with a local anaesthetic for pain. No provincial or territorial health plan pays for it when it is done for non-medical reasons. The CPS position statement behind the handout has since been retired, so ask your doctor for current advice.

If you want it done, raise it with your doctor or midwife early, and ask your masjid which local clinics families use.

sections.heading: After the birth: bleeding and worship
sections.body: Bleeding after childbirth (nifas) follows the same worship rules as a period: you do not pray or fast while it continues, and you make up missed Ramadan fasts later. Our topic on menstruation and worship explains the details and where the schools differ. Follow your doctor's or midwife's advice about your recovery too.

sections.heading: Your mood after the birth
sections.body:
Health Canada reports that 23% of mothers who had recently given birth in Canada described feelings consistent with postpartum depression or an anxiety disorder, a figure from the 2018/2019 Survey on Maternal Health.

Feeling low, anxious or numb after a birth is not weak faith and not ingratitude. Tell your doctor, midwife or public health nurse. Help is available, and Health Canada has published treatment guidelines for these conditions.

If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 911. If you are thinking about suicide or worried about a new parent, call or text 9-8-8.

scripts.title: When a relative insists on a custom
scripts.body: Thank you, I know this means a lot to you. I'm learning which things are from the religion and which are family customs, so let me ask my teacher about this one.

scripts.title: Asking your doctor about circumcision
scripts.body: We are Muslim, and we would like our son to be circumcised for religious reasons. Who do you recommend, what pain relief is used, and what does it cost?

scripts.title: Telling your care provider how you feel
scripts.body: Since the baby came I have been feeling low (or anxious) most days, and it is not getting better. I would like to talk about what help is available.

scenarios.title: You cannot afford an aqiqah.
scenarios.response: Then it is not asked of you now. You can do it later if your situation changes, before the child reaches puberty, or leave it.

scenarios.title: Your in-laws say the baby must have an Arabic name.
scenarios.response: A good meaning is what matters. You can choose a name you both love, Arabic or not, and explain calmly why.

scenarios.title: Someone tells you postpartum sadness means your faith is weak.
scenarios.response: It does not. Talk to your doctor or midwife, and lean on people who support you.

title: Facing hate and harassment
description: What to do if someone targets you for being Muslim: getting safe, keeping a record, where to report in Canada, and looking after yourself afterwards.
intro: Most days pass without trouble. Some Muslims in Canada, especially people who look visibly Muslim, do meet hostility: a shout on the bus, a hand pulling at a hijab, abuse online. If it happens to you, it is not your fault and you do not have to deal with it alone. This guide explains what counts as a hate crime, how to keep a record, where you can report, and what helps afterwards. It is general information, not legal advice.
summary: If you are hurt or still in danger, call 911.
Write down what happened the same day, and save screenshots and photos before you block or delete anything.
You can report to your local police, anonymously to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477, and to the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM). You can do one, two or all three.
Discrimination in housing, in a store or school, or at most workplaces can go to your provincial or territorial human rights agency.
Fear and poor sleep are common afterwards. Victim services can help, and you can call or text 9-8-8 if it becomes too much.

sections.heading: Hate crime or hate incident?
sections.body:
The RCMP explains the difference. A hate crime is a criminal offence, such as an assault, a threat or damage to property, committed out of hate or bias against a group, for example a religion. A hate incident is hateful behaviour that is not a crime, such as a slur or someone mocking your religion on social media.

Both are worth reporting. The RCMP says that reporting incidents, no matter how minor, helps police prevent them. In 2024, police in Canada recorded 229 hate crimes targeting Muslims, according to Statistics Canada.

sections.heading: Right now: get safe
items: Move away from the person and towards other people, a driver, staff or a shop.
If anyone is hurt, or the person is still threatening you, call 911.
Do not confront the person physically. Your safety comes first.
If someone saw what happened, ask for their name and phone number.

sections.heading: Keep a record
sections.body: The Yaqeen Institute authors Imam Khalid Latif, Dr. Salman Khan and Mazin Awad put it simply: documentation matters. A record helps the police, NCCM or a human rights agency, even weeks later. Try to write it down on the same day.
items: The date, the time and the place.
What was said or done, in the person's own words if you can remember them.
What the person looked like, any vehicle, and the names of witnesses.
Screenshots of online abuse, showing the account name and the date. Take them before you block or report the account.
Photos of any injury or damage. Keep damaged items, such as a torn hijab.

sections.heading: Where you can report
sections.body: Reporting is your choice, and you can report to more than one place.
items: Your local police. In an emergency, call 911. Otherwise use your local police non-emergency line or online reporting, or the RCMP detachment if the RCMP polices your area.

Crime Stoppers, if you want to stay anonymous. Call 1-800-222-8477 (1-800-222-TIPS) or use its secure online form. It does not ask for your name and has no caller ID. Crime Stoppers is not the police and does not offer victim support.

The National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM). Anyone who experienced or saw discrimination, harassment or a hate crime can fill in its incident form. NCCM confirms it has your report within seven days, contacts you if the case is one it can take on, and does not share your information without your consent. NCCM is an advocacy group, not the police or a legal service.

Your provincial or territorial human rights agency, for discrimination in housing, in a store or restaurant, in a school or in health care, or at a workplace that is not federally regulated. The Canadian Human Rights Commission links to each agency. In Ontario, for example, the Human Rights Code covers renting a home and being served in stores, schools and on transit.
At college or university, ask the dean of students or the student union which office takes harassment and discrimination reports. Report a crime to the police as well.

sections.heading: Why reporting still helps
sections.body: Many people never report. In a 2019 Statistics Canada survey, only 22% of incidents that people saw as motivated by hate were reported to police. Statistics Canada lists language barriers, trust in police and fear of it happening again among the reasons people stay silent. Those reasons make sense. A report still counts: it is how police and governments see where hate is happening.

sections.heading: After it happens
sections.body:
Justice Canada says people targeted by hate often feel less safe afterwards, and some have anxiety, low mood or trouble sleeping. It can shake your family and your community too. These are common reactions to something that should not have happened.

Justice Canada's Victim Services Directory finds victim services near you by postal code. Tell one person you trust what happened. If fear or poor sleep has not settled after a few weeks, talk to your doctor or a counsellor. If you are thinking about suicide, call or text 9-8-8 at any time.

sections.heading: If you wear hijab
sections.body:
Visible Muslim women, converts included, are often the ones singled out. Dr. Naved Bakali of the University of Windsor interviewed Muslim women about this, including a convert who was abused after she started wearing hijab. Being targeted says nothing wrong about you, your faith or your hijab.

Some women ask whether they may change or remove their hijab in a place where they fear for their safety. That is a question of Islamic law, and this guide does not answer it. Ask a qualified scholar you trust.

sections.heading: Faith alongside practical help
sections.body: Many Muslims find comfort in dua when they are shaken, and the dua page has a section for when you feel anxious or overwhelmed. Making dua and reporting what happened can go together.

scripts.title: Asking a witness for help
scripts.body: Excuse me, did you see what just happened? Could I have your name and number in case the police need a witness?

scripts.title: Starting a police report
scripts.body: I want to report a hate incident. On [date] at [place], a person [what they did or said]. I think it was because I am Muslim. I have photos and a witness.

scripts.title: Telling someone you trust
scripts.body: Something frightening happened to me today. I don't need you to fix it. Can I tell you about it?

scenarios.title: Someone shouts at you about your religion on the bus, then gets off.
scenarios.response: Move near the driver or other passengers. Once you are safe, write down the time, the route and what was said. You can report it to the police and to NCCM.

scenarios.title: A stranger grabs at your hijab in a shop.
scenarios.response: This may be a crime. Get to safety, and call 911 if you are hurt or the person is still there. Ask the staff to keep any security video, and write down what happened.

scenarios.title: Someone posts abuse about you online.
scenarios.response: Take screenshots that show the account, the words and the date before you block or report it. Report it to the platform, to the police if it includes threats, and to NCCM.

scenarios.title: A landlord will not rent to you after seeing you pray.
scenarios.response: That can be discrimination in housing. Write down what was said and keep any messages. Contact your provincial or territorial human rights agency.

title: Coming back after a break
description: If you stopped praying or drifted from Islam for a while: how to return, what scholars say about missed prayers, and walking back into the masjid.
intro: Many Muslims, converts and people raised in the faith alike, go through a stretch when they stop praying or drift away. Coming back is always possible, and it can start with the next prayer. This guide covers the first day back, what scholars say about missed prayers, and walking back into a masjid without owing anyone an explanation.
summary: Allah says not to lose hope in His mercy, for He forgives all sins (Quran 39:53).
Start with the next prayer. You do not need to feel ready first.
Prayers from before you knew prayer was required are not owed.

For prayers missed after that, the relied-upon positions of the four schools require making them up, on a schedule you can keep. Some scholars differed about prayers missed on purpose. Ask a teacher to help you plan.
Nobody at the masjid is owed an explanation for where you have been.

sections.heading: The door is open
sections.body:
Allah says, "O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins" (Quran 39:53, translation of the meaning by Dr. Mustafa Khattab). The Prophet said that if people did not sin, Allah would replace them with people who sin and then ask His forgiveness, and He would forgive them (Sahih Muslim 2749).

Roohi Tahir of the Yaqeen Institute writes that repentance is a way of life. You return to Allah whenever you slip, even after falling again, and despair is one of the main things that keeps people from coming back.

sections.heading: Your first day back
items: Make wudu and pray the next prayer that is due.
Say a short repentance in your own words, in any language.
Do not wait until you feel ready. Pray first.
If you want to, tell one person you trust that you are back.

sections.heading: Missed prayers
sections.body:
Prayers from before you became Muslim are not owed. A SeekersGuidance answer by Ustadha Shaista Maqbool also says a convert in a non-Muslim country is not responsible for prayers from the time before they knew prayer was obligatory.

For prayers missed after that, a SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Dr. Muhammad Fayez Awad says making them up is required, with sincere repentance. It cites Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars, and Ibn Rushd for the majority view. The same answer quotes Ibn Rushd saying scholars differed about someone who missed prayers on purpose, and notes that some scholars differed on whether make-up applies to deliberately missed prayers. If you left Islam for a time and have come back, ask a teacher how this applies to you.

If you make prayers up, go gently. Ustadha Maqbool suggests a schedule you can keep, such as making up one day of prayers each day, even if it takes a year or longer.
items: Estimate the number roughly. Do not let the count stop you praying today.
Add make-up prayers alongside your daily prayers, or follow the schedule your teacher sets.
Do not try to make up months in a few days. A steady plan lasts longer.

sections.heading: Going back to the masjid
sections.body: You do not owe anyone an explanation for where you have been. Walk in, pray, and leave if that is all you can manage today. If someone asks, a short answer is enough. If you felt unwelcome at one masjid before, try another, or a class for new Muslims.

sections.heading: What pulled you away?
sections.body: It can help to name what made you drift, because each reason has its own kind of help.
items: Taking on too much at once: see the plan for hard weeks on the New Muslim basics page.
Loneliness: see the loneliness and belonging guide.
Doubts or faith that feels flat: see the questions and doubts topic.
Low mood that does not lift, or alcohol and drugs: see the mental health page.

scripts.title: A short repentance
scripts.body: O Allah, I stayed away and I am sorry. I am coming back to You. Forgive me and help me keep going.

scripts.title: If someone at the masjid asks
scripts.body: I've been away for a while. It's good to be back.

scripts.title: Asking a friend to check in
scripts.body: I stopped praying for a while, and I'm starting again this week. Could you check in on me now and then?

scenarios.title: You have not prayed in six months and feel too ashamed to start.
scenarios.response: Start with the next prayer, just that one. Repent in your own words. Then ask a teacher to help you plan any make-up prayers.

scenarios.title: You try to make up everything in one weekend and burn out.
scenarios.response: Slow down. A schedule you can keep, such as one day of make-ups each day, works better than a burst you cannot repeat.

scenarios.title: Someone at the masjid says they have not seen you in a while.
scenarios.response: A short, friendly answer is enough. You do not owe anyone your story.
